title: Sean Payton Rules Out Benching Bo Nix, Stands Firm on Starting Quarterback – NBC Sports
body:
The Denver Broncos secured a dramatic overtime victory against the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday night, but the win was quickly eclipsed by a heated debate over the performance of rookie quarterback Bo Nix. Former NFL quarterback and Prime Video analyst Ryan Fitzpatrick blasted Nix’s play as “garbage,” prompting Broncos head coach Sean Payton to publicly defend his young signal‑caller and deny any consideration of benching him. The exchange has reignited discussions about the Broncos’ offensive direction and the patience required to develop a first‑year starter in a competitive AFC West.

The overtime thriller ended with Denver edging Seattle 31‑28, a game that saw the Broncos rally from a 17‑point deficit. Nix, who entered the contest as a starter for the first time this season, completed 18 of 30 passes for 219 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception. While the statistics suggest a respectable effort for a rookie, Fitzpatrick focused on the quarterback’s early struggles, including a series of errant throws and a lack of poise in the red zone. “He was playing garbage ball for the first half,” the analyst said during the post‑game broadcast, adding that the Broncos “can’t afford to keep giving the ball to a kid who isn’t ready.”

Payton, who took the helm in Denver last season after a successful tenure with the New Orleans Saints, responded on social media, emphasizing that he has not contemplated removing Nix from the lineup. “We’re in the process of developing Bo. He’s learning, growing, and we’ll continue to give him the reps he needs,” the coach wrote, adding that the team’s focus remains on building a cohesive offense rather than reacting to external criticism. Payton’s stance reflects a broader trend in the NFL, where teams are increasingly patient with young quarterbacks, recognizing that early setbacks can be part of a longer developmental curve.

The controversy highlights the delicate balance between performance expectations and developmental patience. Denver entered the season with a roster that blends veteran talent—such as running back Javonte Williams and wide receiver Courtland Sutton—with a relatively inexperienced quarterback corps. The Broncos’ front office invested a second‑round pick in Nix, hoping his dual‑threat skill set would eventually complement the team’s run‑heavy identity. Critics argue that the Broncos’ offensive line has struggled to protect Nix consistently, forcing him into uncomfortable throws, while supporters point to his composure in the final minutes as evidence of his potential.

Analysts also note that the Broncos’ coaching staff has made adjustments to better suit Nix’s strengths. In the second half, Denver incorporated more roll‑out passes and play‑action concepts, allowing Nix to exploit his mobility and buy time for his receivers to get open. The successful go‑ahead drive in overtime, capped by a 12‑yard touchdown pass to tight end Albert Okwuegbunam, demonstrated the effectiveness of these tweaks. However, the early missteps—particularly a sack that resulted in a fumble—underscore the learning curve still ahead.

Looking ahead, the Broncos will face a crucial stretch of divisional games that could define Nix’s trajectory. If the team can shore up protection and continue to tailor the playbook to his skill set, the rookie may solidify his role as the franchise’s long‑term starter. Conversely, sustained criticism from high‑profile analysts could increase pressure on both Nix and the coaching staff, potentially accelerating a reevaluation of the quarterback depth chart. For now, Payton’s reassurance signals that Denver is willing to endure growing pains, trusting that the experience gained in close contests like Thursday’s overtime win will ultimately pay dividends as the Broncos chase a playoff berth.
